title: CVE-2022-35260: .netrc parser out-of-bounds access
explain: The code supports the reported flaw. A maintainer should review its impact and decide what to do next.

grounding.rev_source: release curl-7_85_0 (fits the report's line numbers and quotes better than master on 2022-10-03)

summary: Curl expects the .netrc file to have space characters; if it lacks spaces, parsenetrc() performs out-of-bounds reads and a 1-byte out-of-bounds write, potentially causing crashes or other consequences.

claims.text: parsenetrc() performs an out-of-bounds read when encountering non-space characters in the .netrc file.
claims.reasoning: The loop at line 111 increments tok_end while the character is not a space. With a .netrc file containing 4095 'a' bytes and no newline, fgets fills netrcbuffer[0..4094] with 'a' and places '\0' at netrcbuffer[4095]. Since ISSPACE('\0') is false (Curl_isspace(0) returns 0), the loop reads netrcbuffer[4095] (valid), increments tok_end to 4096, then reads netrcbuffer[4096] (out-of-bounds) for the next iteration's condition check.

citations.note: while(!ISSPACE(*tok_end)) tok_end++; reads past the buffer when no space character exists in the netrcbuffer
tok_end increments without bounds check; fgets guarantees null-termination at netrcbuffer[4095] but ISSPACE('\0') is false, so loop continues past buffer end

claims.text: parsenetrc() performs a 1-byte out-of-bounds write at line 27.
claims.reasoning: After the while(!ISSPACE(*tok_end)) loop exits (when it randomly encounters a byte that ISSPACE considers a space), line 113 writes a null terminator at that out-of-bounds tok_end position. This is a 1-byte out-of-bounds write.

citations.note: *tok_end = 0; writes a null byte at the position where the loop stopped, which can be one or more bytes past the 4096-byte buffer

claims.text: A .netrc file consisting of 4095 bytes of the character 'a' (no space or newline) can trigger the flaw.
claims.reasoning: A 4095-byte file of 'a' with no newline causes fgets to fill the entire buffer (indices 0-4094 = 'a', index 4095 = '\0'). Since 'a' and '\0' are both non-space, the tok_end loop runs past the buffer end. Smaller files can also trigger it if memory after the buffer lacks space characters.

citations.note: char netrcbuffer[4096]; buffer size is 4096 bytes
fgets(netrcbuffer, netrcbuffsize, file) reads at most 4095 chars + null terminator

claims.text: Application crash plus other as yet undetermined consequences.
claims.reasoning: Buffer overrun reads and writes are undefined behavior in C and can cause application crashes, memory corruption, or potential code execution depending on heap layout.

claims.text: Running `curl --netrc-file .netrc test.local` with a .netrc file of 4095 'a' bytes reproduces the issue.
claims.reasoning: The --netrc-file command line option triggers parsenetrc() with the attacker-controlled .netrc file, making the reproduction steps accurate.

citations.note: parsenetrc is called when --netrc-file option is used

key_reasons: The while(!ISSPACE(*tok_end)) loop at lib/netrc.c:111 lacks a bounds check against the netrcbuffer end.
fgets guarantees null-termination within the 4096-byte buffer, but ISSPACE('\0') is false, so the loop continues past the buffer.
The subsequent *tok_end = 0 at line 113 writes a null byte out-of-bounds.
An attacker controlling the .netrc file content (via --netrc-file) can trigger this reliably with a file containing no whitespace characters.
reply: Thank you for the detailed report. The vulnerability is confirmed: in lib/netrc.c, the loop at line 111 (while(!ISSPACE(*tok_end)) tok_end++;) lacks a bounds check, allowing tok_end to run past the 4096-byte netrcbuffer when the .netrc file contains no whitespace. The write at line 113 (*tok_end = 0;) then writes a null byte out-of-bounds. A 4095-byte file of 'a' with no newline reliably triggers this. We will prepare a fix adding a buffer-end check to the loop condition.
